explanations.answer: She becomes queen in place of Vashti
explanations.explanation: The attendants say it plainly: “Then let the young woman who pleases the king become queen in place of Vashti.” (Esther 2:4) Vashti is the queen being replaced. So this plan isn't just a talent show. The winner gets the crown.

explanations.answer: She rules over her home province
explanations.explanation: Nobody in this plan gets a province and a little flag to wave. The commissioners gather the young women from the provinces into the harem at Susa, so they travel in, not out. The prize the attendants name is this: “…become queen in place of Vashti.” (Esther 2:4) Pretty big promotion from a home province.

explanations.answer: She joins the king's royal council
explanations.explanation: A seat at the council table is a fine thing, but the attendants never offer it. Their plan ends with one job opening. The young woman who pleases the king becomes “…queen in place of Vashti.” (Esther 2:4) Vashti is the queen being replaced.
The text says it straight: “This suggestion pleased the king, and he acted accordingly.” (Esther 2:4) King Xerxes hears the plan and says yes. I wish my own ideas got that kind of green light.
This one is true, friend. Esther 2:4 says, “This suggestion pleased the king, and he acted accordingly.” King Xerxes doesn't just tolerate the plan, he likes it. Then he acts on it.

explanations.answer: She has no father or mother
explanations.explanation: Esther 2:7 says Mordecai brought her up “…because she did not have a father or mother.” Mordecai is the Jewish man from the tribe of Benjamin, and Esther is the daughter of his uncle. So she's his cousin, and he takes her as his own daughter. That's what family does.

explanations.answer: Her parents live far away in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Her parents aren't in Jerusalem, friend. The text says she “…did not have a father or mother.” and that her father and mother had died. (Esther 2:7) Jerusalem is where Mordecai was carried into exile from, not where her parents are.

explanations.answer: Her father serves in the king's palace
explanations.explanation: Esther doesn't end up in the palace through her father. The text says she had no father or mother, and that they had died. (Esther 2:7) She only gets to the palace when she's taken there after the king's edict goes out.

Mordecai didn't take her in as a servant. Esther 2:7 says that when her father and mother had died, “…Mordecai had taken her as his own daughter.” That's a home with a family in it. A servant doesn't get that line.
Right, it's false. Esther 2:7 says Mordecai “…had taken her as his own daughter.” That's a daughter in the house, not a servant. Esther lost her parents, and Mordecai made room for her.
Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the women, takes to Esther. Esther 2:9 says she “…pleased him and obtained his favor…” Then he gets busy on her behalf. Nice to have somebody in your corner.

Ignoring her would be the opposite of what happens. Esther 2:9 says she “…pleased him and obtained his favor…” Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the women, acts fast for her. Nobody gets ignored when they're handed seven maidservants.

Hegai doesn't send her home. The text says she “…pleased him and obtained his favor…” so he gives her beauty treatments, a special diet and seven select maidservants. (Esther 2:9) Esther stays, and he moves her to the best place in the harem.

Esther 2:9 says Hegai “…transferred her with them to the best place in the harem.” Her seven select maidservants go along too. That's an upgrade with a whole team. I'd have been happy with a window that opens.
Smallest isn't the word the text uses. Esther 2:9 says Hegai moved her “…to the best place in the harem.” Her seven select maidservants go with her.

The text never says anything about quiet. Esther 2:9 says Hegai moved her “…to the best place in the harem.” It could be a nice quiet spot, but the verse only calls it the best. I'll stick to what the verse says.

That one is false, friend. Esther 2:10 says, “Esther did not reveal her people or her lineage, because Mordecai had instructed her not to do so.” She doesn't reveal either one, so she isn't telling everyone.
Right, it's false. Esther 2:10 says, “Esther did not reveal her people or her lineage, because Mordecai had instructed her not to do so.” In the palace, she keeps both to herself.

explanations.answer: Mordecai told her not to tell
explanations.explanation: Esther 2:10 gives the reason: “…because Mordecai had instructed her not to do so.” Mordecai is the one who raised her, and she listens to him. The verse doesn't say why he gave the instruction, so I won't guess.
No servants step in here. The verse gives one reason: “…because Mordecai had instructed her not to do so.” (Esther 2:10) The person who gave the instruction is the man who raised her.
The reason in Esther 2:10 is a person, not a law. She kept quiet “…because Mordecai had instructed her not to do so.” That's the man who raised her, and his instruction is the reason the verse gives.

explanations.answer: Walks back and forth outside the harem court
explanations.explanation: Esther 2:11 says, “…every day Mordecai would walk back and forth in front of the court of the harem…” He does it to learn about Esther's welfare and what's happening to her. I think a man who does that every single day cares a lot.

explanations.answer: Sends letters to Esther in the harem
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a letter. Mordecai goes himself. Esther 2:11 says he would “…walk back and forth in front of the court of the harem…” every day, to learn about Esther's welfare. That's a lot of steps.

explanations.answer: Waits outside the king's throne room
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but Mordecai isn't at the throne room. He's walking back and forth “…in front of the court of the harem…” where Esther is. (Esther 2:11) He's checking on her, not on the king.

Esther 2:13 says the young woman “…was given whatever she requested to take with her from the harem to the king’s palace.” The choice is left with her. The verse doesn't say what any woman asked for, so I'll leave that open. That's a generous send-off.

The verse puts the choice in her hands. She “…was given whatever she requested to take with her from the harem to the king’s palace.” (Esther 2:13) The king isn't sending a list. She makes the request.

explanations.answer: Nothing from the harem at all
explanations.explanation: Nothing isn't what the verse says. Esther 2:13 says the young woman “…was given whatever she requested to take with her from the harem to the king’s palace.” Whatever she requests is allowed, and that's the opposite of nothing at all.

That's exactly how it works. Esther 2:14 says she “…would not return to the king unless he delighted in her and summoned her by name.” Two things have to be true: he delights in her, and he summons her by name. Nobody shows up twice by accident.

This one is true. Esther 2:14 says she “…would not return to the king unless he delighted in her and summoned her by name.” Two things have to happen first. He has to delight in her, and he has to call her by name.

Esther 2:15 says she asked for nothing “…except what Hegai, the king’s trusted official in charge of the harem, had advised.” She takes his advice and leaves it there. You know that friend who skips the long list and just trusts the one who knows? That's Esther here.

Shaashgaz is the king's eunuch in charge of the concubines, and the young women go to him after their night with the king. (Esther 2:14) Esther's advice comes from someone else. Esther 2:15 says she asked for nothing “except what Hegai…had advised.”

Carshena is one of the nobles named in Esther 1:14, and he isn't in this scene at all. The one Esther listens to is Hegai. Esther 2:15 says she asked for nothing “…except what Hegai, the king’s trusted official in charge of the harem, had advised.”
It's not just a few people. Esther 2:15 says, “…Esther found favor in the eyes of everyone who saw her.” The word is everyone, so no one is left out. That's a whole lot of favor.

Right, it's false. Esther 2:15 says, “…Esther found favor in the eyes of everyone who saw her.” EVERYONE. Not a few, not most, everyone. I've stood in a bakery line where I couldn't get three people to agree on a cookie, so that's a lot of agreeing.

Esther 2:17 says, “…the king loved Esther more than all the other women…” More than all the other women is a big statement. It says she found grace and favor in his sight, too. That's why the crown goes to her.
This one is true. Esther 2:17 says, “…the king loved Esther more than all the other women…” She finds “…grace and favor in his sight more than all of the other virgins.” Out of everyone, it's Esther.

Esther 2:17 says, “…he placed the royal crown upon her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.” Not on a pillow, not in a box, but on her head. Now it's official, and Vashti's seat has someone new in it.
No robe shows up in this verse. Esther 2:17 says, “…he placed the royal crown upon her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.” A robe might look nice on a queen, but the king places the crown.
A ring isn't mentioned here at all. In this passage, the king “…placed the royal crown upon her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.” (Esther 2:17) It's the crown that does the job.
Esther 2:18 says the king “…proclaimed a tax holiday in the provinces…” I bet that one got a cheer. It comes with the banquet and the gifts.
There's no parade in the verse. Esther 2:18 says the king held a great banquet and “…proclaimed a tax holiday in the provinces…” Bills are a lot more fun to skip than floats are to watch.

The verse doesn't mention a census. Esther 2:18 says the king “…proclaimed a tax holiday in the provinces…” A census is about counting people, and a tax holiday is about taxes. That's what the king proclaims.

She's queen now, but nothing changes on this point. Esther 2:20 says, “Esther still had not revealed her lineage or her people, just as Mordecai had instructed.” The crown doesn't loosen her lips. She keeps what Mordecai asked.

Right, it's false. Esther 2:20 says, “Esther still had not revealed her lineage or her people, just as Mordecai had instructed.” Even with the crown, she says nothing. She does what Mordecai told her.

Esther 2:22 says, “When Mordecai learned of the plot, he reported it to Queen Esther…” Mordecai is sitting at the king's gate, and Esther is the queen he brings it to. She's the one who carries it to the king.
Memucan is a name from earlier, when he spoke up before the king in Esther 1:16. He isn't in this scene. Mordecai takes the news to someone else. Esther 2:22 says, “…he reported it to Queen Esther…”
Harbona is one of the king's eunuchs named in Esther 1:10, but he doesn't show up here. Esther 2:22 says Mordecai “…reported it to Queen Esther…” She's the one who gets the news.
Esther 2:22 says “…she informed the king on Mordecai’s behalf.” Mordecai learned of the plot and reported it to Queen Esther. She is the one who informs the king, and she does it for him.
This one is true. Esther 2:22 says “…she informed the king on Mordecai’s behalf.” Mordecai learned of the plot, and Esther carried it to the king for him.

I think this part is heavy, so I'll say it simply. Esther 2:23 says that after the report was investigated and verified, “…both officials were hanged on the gallows.” Bigthan and Teresh are the two who plotted against the king. The report had been checked first.

This is a heavy part of the story, and exile isn't what the text says. Esther 2:23 says that after the report was investigated and verified, “…both officials were hanged on the gallows.” The text doesn't say anything about exile.

I think this is a heavy moment, and prison isn't in the text. Esther 2:23 says that after the report was investigated and verified, “…both officials were hanged on the gallows.” The plot was taken seriously, and the report was checked first.

explanations.answer: It's written in the king's records
explanations.explanation: Esther 2:23 says, “…all this was recorded in the Book of the Chronicles in the presence of the king.” It's written down right in front of him. A line in the books, not a billboard. And the story isn't over.

The text doesn't mention an announcement. Esther 2:23 says, “…all this was recorded in the Book of the Chronicles in the presence of the king.” What it gives is a record in the king's book, with the king there.

explanations.answer: It's carved on the king's gate
explanations.explanation: Mordecai is sitting at the king's gate, but the text doesn't mention anything being carved on it. Esther 2:23 says, “…all this was recorded in the Book of the Chronicles in the presence of the king.” The record goes in a book, and the king is there.
